title: Infinite game development
author: Golgorz
selftext: This is happening to me....making a mobile game, started with an old simple idea..starting development and while doing it and finishing features...new ideas or big improvements comes to mi mind...do a test, it works...implement it...come up with new ideas or big changes...test..implement, re-implement the new idea with a new idea...and this happens almost everytime...just like...why not try? hahahaha ....started with a wooden house and builing a skyscrapper.... does this happen to you too?? ( i know i have to put limits and so on...but as this is a hobby....why not try?)

comments.author: Livid_Shallot5701
comments.body: yes. currently im backtracking almost half my game features since "hm, this would be cool, ask agent if this would work, he tells me its easy and 0,1ms increase, has 50% of it finished anyway to tell me, might as well implement it" -> a lot of stuff that is cool, but it takes away from the actual gameplay in a sense that its too much to be able to do 10 different things to a tree when every player just wants to cut it for wood

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body: I feel ya. I can’t get past the first 10 minutes of my game becuse every time I play I think of a dozen fixes, improvements, or new features. Exaggerating a bit, but my task list is growing like wild. It’s a good problem to have though, endless fun ideas to experiment with. I think it’s actually good to run wild for a while just add tons of stuff, see what works, then pare it back to the essentials and polish it all.

comments.author: 32b1b46b6befce6ab149
comments.body: it's called "scope creep" and it's well known in development circles.

comments.author: IronDrop
comments.body:
This is exactly why 99% of indie game devs used to fail and not publish their game. It's called "scope creep". You endlessly want to add things to your game, ending up with something that has either become impossible to maintain or you've gone so far out of your original concept that it's just become something horrendous that tries to be everything and nothing at once. This is why some people have developed methods.

Learn how to make a GDD. A Game Design Document where you'll put everything you want your game to be with a precise roadmap. You give a hierarchy to the tasks and implement things by priority. AND YOU STICK TO IT. If everyone did that, far more games would get released.

Search Youtube for how to create a GDD and I promise this will be the most valueable thing you'll learn today.

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: As most have already said "Scope Creep", but what's the opposite? That's the hard part, deciding what to leave out and when to stop. But as a hobby? No reason you can't work on something forever if you enjoy it and and the endless changes. Could be a source of smaller focused games.

comments.author: ImCallingYouOutOnBS
comments.body: More does not always mean better

comments.author: Officialpolygrafix
comments.body:
If you're new to game dev, thats what we call "Feature creep". If you ever heard that phrase but never knew what it meant, now you do.   
at some point you have to settle with what you think is "good enough" and ship it. Then market it. get players on it. I personally guarantee that whatever features and improvements you put in that you love, there will be a significant amount of players going "meh.." and that they too will be coming up with features you haven't thought of but want implemented. So set a deadline, stick to that deadline, and ship it. Then wait to hear what the players say.

comments.author: CandidateDue2480
comments.body: This is an extremely common process. It's one of the key things an inexperienced developer can't stop themselves from doing and leads to never finishing any games, as controlling scope and closing a product are harder and less fun than the initial ideas.

I don't want more features, I want to become more efficient. So I told Claude "at the end of each task, reflect how you could've done it faster."
